inline.s: The Buddha asked Subhuti: What do you think? In former days, at the place of Dipankara Buddha, did the Tathāgata obtain any dharma? Subhuti answered: No, World-Honored One! At the place of Dipankara Buddha the Tathāgata did not obtain any dharma.

[Dipankara Buddha] Also translated as the Lamp-Lighting Buddha, the Buddha of Universal Light, and the Buddha of Fixed Light. [In former days, at the place of Dipankara Buddha] In the past, when the World-Honored One was a bodhisattva of the seventh ground, he met Dipankara Buddha and heard the Dharma, realized the patient endurance of the non-arising of dharmas, and ascended to the eighth ground; Dipankara Buddha then gave him the prophecy, saying: After ninety-one kalpas, in the kalpa called the Auspicious Kalpa, you shall attain Buddhahood, with the name Shakyamuni. [Prophecy] The Buddha's beforehand recording of a bodhisattva's name: after how many ages, in what place and what land, he will become what Buddha. [Auspicious Kalpa] The past great kalpa is called the Adorned Kalpa, the future great kalpa is called the Star Constellation Kalpa, and the present great kalpa is called the Auspicious Kalpa, because in this great kalpa a thousand Buddhas appear in the world.

[At the place of Dipankara Buddha the Tathāgata in truth obtained no dharma] Here “in truth obtained no dharma” has two meanings. Ultimately speaking, all that is in the dream of ignorance is illusion, and so in truth no dharma whatever is obtained. At the same time, the Tathāgata, while on the causal ground, did not cling to there being anything to obtain: he cultivated without cultivating, attained without attaining, and so was able to realize the fruit of Buddhahood. In the Buddha Treasury Sutra

Chapter Eight, on Pure Seeing, the World-Honored One tells in detail of his own practice on the causal ground: for a span of kalpas exceedingly long, because he clung to there being something to obtain, the Buddhas did not give him a prophecy. For example:

“The Buddha said to Shariputra: I recall that in past ages, seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I met thirty billion Buddhas, all named Shakyamuni, and each time I served them as a wheel-turning sage king to the end of my life, and likewise their disciples, with clothing, food, bedding, and medicine, seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; yet those Buddhas did not prophesy of me, ‘In a future life you shall become a Buddha.’ Why? Because I had something to obtain. Shariputra, I recall that in past ages, in the seven hundredth asaṃkhyeya kalpa, I met a thousand Buddhas, all named Jambu Gold, and to the end of my life I made the four offerings to them, and they likewise did not prophesy of me, because I had something to obtain. Shariputra, I recall that in past ages, also in the seven hundredth asaṃkhyeya kalpa, I met six million two hundred thousand Buddhas, all named See-All-Meaning, and each time I served them as a wheel-turning sage king, with every kind of enjoyable thing to the end of my life, and likewise their disciples, and they likewise did not prophesy of me, because I had something to obtain.”
[Causal ground] From the stage of an ordinary being first arousing the mind to learn the Buddha-way, up until the perfection of Buddhahood, this whole course is called the “causal ground.”
This makes clear that the dharma the Tathāgata obtained is illusion, not to be clung to: it breaks the mark of dharmas.

In the preceding section Subhuti answered rightly that the four fruits (the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the fruit of arhatship) are all such that in truth no dharma is obtained. Now the World-Honored One, taking his own practice on the causal ground as an example, further clarifies the wondrous principle that “in truth no dharma is obtained”: not only are the four fruits of the hearers such that nothing is obtained, but even the Buddha-fruit I have realized is such that in truth nothing is obtained. The counter-question was asked in order to bring Subhuti to an inner understanding and so help beings cut through delusion layer by layer.
In the Great Prajñā-Pāramitā Sūtra
Volume Five Hundred Seventy-one
Chapter Six
Chapter Nine, on Non-Attainment, “non-attainment” is set forth in detail:
“At that time in the assembly there was a great bodhisattva named Well-Versed in Thought, who asked Superior
(Superior Heaven King)

saying: ‘Has the Buddha given the Heaven King the bodhi prophecy?’ Superior answered: ‘Though I have received the prophecy, it is still like a dream.’ Then Well-Versed in Thought asked Superior again: ‘When the Heaven King received the prophecy, what did he obtain?’ Superior answered: ‘Though I have received the prophecy, I obtained nothing.’ Well-Versed in Thought said again: ‘He who obtains nothing—what dharma does he not obtain?’ Superior replied: ‘He who obtains nothing does not obtain a self, does not obtain a being, and up to does not obtain a knower or a seer; he does not obtain the aggregates
(the five aggregates: form, feeling, perception, formation, and consciousness)
or the realms
(the eighteen realms; the six faculties, the six dusts, and the six consciousnesses together are called the eighteen realms)
, or the fields

(the twelve fields: the six faculties plus the six dusts are together called the twelve fields. “Field” means the place of production: from the six faculties meeting the six dusts, the six consciousnesses are produced)

, whether good or not good, defiled or pure, with outflows or without outflows, worldly or world-transcending, conditioned or unconditioned, birth-and-death or nirvāṇa—in all such things he obtains nothing.’”
The Heart Sutra says:

“Therefore, in emptiness there is no form, no feeling, perception, formation, or consciousness; no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas; no realm of eye, and so on up to no realm of mind-consciousness; no ignorance, and no extinction of ignorance, and so on up to no aging-and-death, and no extinction of aging-and-death; no suffering, accumulation, extinction, or path; no wisdom; and no attainment. Because there is nothing to attain, the bodhisattva, relying on prajñā-pāramitā, has no obstruction in the mind. Because there is no obstruction, there is no fear; far removed from inverted dreams, he reaches ultimate nirvāṇa.”

This says that the five aggregates, the eighteen realms, the dharmas of the twelve links of conditioned co-arising, the dharmas of the Four Noble Truths, and the dharmas of the six perfections are all without attainment. (For details see
A Detailed Explanation of the Heart Sutra
Subhuti! What do you think? Does a bodhisattva adorn the Buddha-land? No, World-Honored One! Why? What is called the adornment of Buddha-lands is not adornment; therefore it is called adornment.

The Buddha asked Subhuti: Subhuti! What do you think? Does a bodhisattva, cultivating the six perfections and ten thousand practices, adorn the Buddha-land? Subhuti answered: There is no adorning of the Buddha-land, World-Honored One! Why is there not? Because adorning the Buddha-land is an affair within the dream of ignorance: it has marks but no substance, and is an illusion.

[Adorning the Buddha-land] To adorn is to decorate richly. When a bodhisattva on the causal ground cultivates the six perfections and ten thousand practices and dedicates this merit to adorning the land of his dependent retribution when he becomes a Buddha, this is called “adorning the Buddha-land.” [The two retributions] Dependent retribution and direct retribution. Dependent retribution is the karmic result on which beings depend for their dwelling, such as lands, the great earth, houses, and implements; direct retribution is the body falsely assembled from the five aggregates, which beings sense as the result of delusion creating karma.

In the sentence “What is called the adornment of Buddha-lands is not adornment; therefore it is called adornment,” “what is called the adornment of Buddha-lands” means that as to marks, there is such a thing as adorning the Buddha-land. “Is not adornment” means that in reality there is no such thing as adorning the Buddha-land, because adorning the Buddha-land is an affair within the dream of ignorance and is not truly existent; this is called having no substance (no substantial reality). “Therefore it is called adornment” means: this illusion, having marks but no substance, is what people call the adornment of Buddha-lands.

In the fifth section the Buddha said: “All marks whatsoever are false and vain.” Hence throughout the sutra the form of statement “having marks, no substance, is illusion” is repeatedly used to judge illusions. For example: “What is called the adornment of Buddha-lands (having marks) is not adornment (no substance); therefore it is called adornment (is illusion).” This is the famous three-part formula “is (having marks), is not (no substance), therefore (what has marks but no substance is illusion).”

What is called the adornment of Buddha-lands is not adornment; therefore it is called adornment”—here too there are two meanings. Ultimately speaking, all that is in the dream of ignorance is illusion, and so indeed it is not adornment. At the same time, only when the bodhisattva does not cling to this is what he cultivates merit, and only so can he adorn the Buddha-land; if the bodhisattva clings to this, then what he cultivates is outflows-tainted merit (outflow is another name for affliction; with outflows means with affliction) and cannot adorn the Buddha-land. Therefore it is said: What is called the adornment of Buddha-lands is not adornment; therefore it is called adornment.
This makes clear that adorning the Buddha-land is illusion, not to be clung to: it breaks the mark of dharmas.

Therefore, Subhuti! All bodhisattvas and great bodhisattvas should thus give rise to the pure mind: they should not give rise to a mind dwelling in form, nor give rise to a mind dwelling in sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas; they should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere.

One should not give rise to a mind of discursive thought dwelling in the six dusts, but should, detached from marks, give rise to the pure mind—this is the essential secret of practice. Now the World-Honored One teaches: “All bodhisattvas and great bodhisattvas should thus give rise to the pure mind: they should not give rise to a mind dwelling in form, nor give rise to a mind dwelling in sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas; they should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere (and should give rise to the mind in a way that dwells nowhere).”
[And should give rise to the mind in a way that dwells nowhere] This says that no thought that arises should cling to marks.
Therefore, Subhuti! All bodhisattvas and great bodhisattvas should thus give rise to the pure mind”
—therefore, Subhuti! All great bodhisattvas should thus give rise to the pure mind.

Therefore” is a summarizing word that carries on the above and opens the following. The World-Honored One told Subhuti: As was said above, the dharma the Tathāgata obtained is illusion, and the bodhisattva's cultivation adorning the Buddha-land is also illusion. Therefore, understanding that all marks are illusion, that in truth there is nothing done and nothing obtained, all bodhisattvas and great bodhisattvas should thus give rise to the pure mind: “They should not give rise to a mind dwelling in form, nor give rise to a mind dwelling in sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas; they should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere.” We beings, since the beginningless kalpa, have turned through the six paths and endured every torment, simply because we give rise to mind by clinging to marks—and what we cling to is illusion. What an immense injustice! So the Diamond Sutra lays bare the truth and dissolves my deluded thoughts of a billion kalpas.

[Bodhisattvas and great bodhisattvas] That is, great bodhisattvas. Here “all bodhisattvas and great bodhisattvas,” as in the third section, refers to the good men and good women who have aroused the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; this appellation expresses the World-Honored One's boundless expectation of them. [Should thus give rise to the pure mind] All the above are illusion; all bodhisattvas and great bodhisattvas should therefore no longer be turned by conditions or by dharmas, but should be their own masters before conditions and dharmas: “no further mark of a self, mark of a human, mark of a being, mark of a life; no mark of dharmas, and no mark of non-dharmas.”

Since the Tathāgata's dharma is unattainable and the bodhisattva's adorning of the Buddha-land is also not something that can be done, and all is illusion, what desire or obstruction remains? So the great bodhisattvas should cultivate the pure mind according to “they should not give rise to a mind dwelling in form, nor give rise to a mind dwelling in sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas; they should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere,” not bewildered by marks, not turned by conditions; only so can they awaken from the great dream. Practice is precisely the cultivation of the pure mind. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
“Detached from marks outwardly is Chan, undisturbed inwardly is concentration; outer Chan and inner concentration—this is Chan concentration.”
They should not give rise to a mind dwelling in form, nor give rise to a mind dwelling in sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas; they should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere”

—one should not, clinging to the dusts of conditions (the dust of form, the dust of sound, the dust of fragrance, the dust of taste, the dust of touch, the dust of dharmas), give rise to a mind of discursive thought (the mind of discrimination and calculation, of love and hate, grasping and rejecting); one should, dwelling nowhere, give rise to the pure mind (one should, dwelling nowhere, give rise to a mind not defiled by the dusts of conditions).

Here “dwell” means to cling to marks and give rise to a discriminating mind—falsely grasping the marks of conditions as real, and so loving, hating, grasping, and rejecting. “Give rise to mind” means to give rise to thoughts. To give rise to mind by clinging to marks is delusion; to give rise to mind without clinging to marks is wisdom. Here “grasping” means seeking; “rejecting” means avoiding. The Great Compendium of a Hundred Commentaries on the Diamond Sutra says:

“The mind of a bodhisattva is always empty and still, without any deluded thoughts, neither arising nor ceasing, unmoving and unshaken—this is the pure mind. The mind of an ordinary being rises and ceases with ignorance, is inverted in deluded thought, grasps and rejects good and evil, and holds views of ordinary being and sage—this is called the turbid and confused mind. ‘They should not give rise to a mind dwelling in form’ means: if the mind is pure, it is not deluded and confused by any condition.”
They should not give rise to a mind dwelling in form, nor give rise to a mind dwelling in sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas; they should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere.”

These are two levels of attainment. “They should not give rise to a mind dwelling in form, nor give rise to a mind dwelling in sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas” means that toward conditions no thought arises; “they should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere” means that though thoughts arise, one does not dwell on them (one does not take form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and dharmas as real).

Not dwelling in form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas when giving rise to mind—this is the state of Chan Master Wolun in the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch: “Toward conditions the mind does not arise.” This too is a state of a certain height, but it has concentration without wisdom, and so is not yet ultimate. Giving rise to a mind that dwells nowhere is the Sixth Patriarch's state of “toward conditions the mind arises again and again,” the state of concentration and wisdom equally held, which is what the Vimalakīrti Nirdeśa Sūtra
Chapter One, on the Buddha-land, says:
“He well discriminates the marks of all dharmas, yet in the supreme meaning he does not move.”
(He can clearly discern the ten thousand dharmas, yet his mind is not moved by these illusions.) This is also what the Sixth Patriarch said:
“Though the six faculties
(eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind)
have seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, they are not defiled by the ten thousand conditions, and the true nature is forever at ease.”
[Supreme meaning] The highest principle, that is, the true character of all dharmas. The Buddha said:

“All dharmas are false; wherever they cease, that is called the real, is called the true character, is called the dharma-realm, is named ultimate wisdom, is named the truth of the supreme meaning, is named the emptiness of the supreme meaning.”
(The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra
Volume Forty
Chapter on Kaundinya)
[They should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere]

“Dwell” means to dwell on and cling—to take conditions and objects as real (clinging to marks). “Dwell nowhere” means not to take any condition or object as real (detached from marks). “They should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere” means: one should give rise to the mind without taking any condition or object as real (detached from marks), which is also what the later scripture, “Chapter Fourteen, on Detachment from Marks and Still Extinction,” calls “one should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere.” This mind that dwells nowhere is the pure mind of a bodhisattva who, within the dream, knows it is a dream. (This sutra says:
“All bodhisattvas and great bodhisattvas should thus give rise to the
pure mind
: they should not give rise to a mind dwelling in form, nor give rise to a mind dwelling in sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas; they should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere.”
) Master Taixu said:
“The mind within the dream is the mind of an ordinary being;
the mind that within the dream knows it is a dream is the mind of a bodhisattva
; the mind awakened from the dream is the mind of a Buddha.”
(An Outline of the Contemplation of Consciousness-Only) Therefore this sutra says:
“If a bodhisattva has the mark of a self, the mark of a human, the mark of a being, or the mark of a life, he is not a bodhisattva.” “If a bodhisattva gives without dwelling in marks
(giving while dwelling nowhere)
, his merit is inconceivable.” “The bodhisattva, with respect to dharmas, should
dwell nowhere
, and practice giving.” “Good men and good women who arouse the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi
should thus give rise to the mind
: I should liberate all beings, and when all beings have been liberated, not one being has in fact been liberated
(liberating beings while dwelling nowhere)
The Great Prajñā-Pāramitā Sūtra
Volume One
Chapter on Learning and Contemplation says:
“All bodhisattvas and great bodhisattvas should, with
non-attachment
(dwelling nowhere)
as the skillful means, perfect prajñā-pāramitā, because the natures and marks of all dharmas are unattainable.”
“Non-attachment” is not clinging to marks, which is detachment from marks.
The Fourth Patriarch of Chan, Daoxin, said:

“Conditions and objects have no beauty or ugliness; beauty and ugliness arise in the mind. If the mind does not forcibly name them, from where do deluded feelings arise? Since deluded feelings do not arise, the true mind freely knows all.”
Here “if the mind does not forcibly name them” is precisely giving rise to the pure mind while dwelling nowhere.
Maitreya Bodhisattva said:
“Discrimination is consciousness; non-discrimination is wisdom. Relying on consciousness one is defiled; relying on wisdom one is pure. Defilement has birth and death; purity has no Buddhas.”
(The Dream Wandering Collection
A Veritable Record of the Old Man Hanshan's Own Prefaced Chronology)
The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch
Chapter Four, on Concentration and Wisdom, says:
“The deluded person has thoughts toward conditions, and upon those thoughts gives rise to wrong views, and from this all the dusts, toils, and deluded thoughts are born.”

Therefore one should not cling to conditions and give rise to mind, that is, “one should not give rise to a mind dwelling in form, nor give rise to a mind dwelling in sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas.”

They should not give rise to a mind dwelling in form, nor give rise to a mind dwelling in sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas”—for those who recite the Buddha's name this is of the utmost importance. The layman Jiang Weannong says in his Lectures on the Diamond Sutra:

“‘They should not dwell’ means that the student should be aware and illuminating upon consciousness, and not give rise to clinging and discrimination.” “In the work of Buddha-recitation, though one may not yet be able to recite without reciting, yet if one's vows and practice are true and earnest, then relying on Amitābha's power of compassionate vows, one will also be received and guided to rebirth, and will at once be equal to the stage of non-retrogression—in Chinese, ‘non-retrogression,’ that is, the stage of the first abiding. To reach this stage by other practices requires passing through distant kalpas; now it is brought to accomplishment in a single life—how much more need be said of its being the most skillful of skillful means! . . . Yet for vows and practice to be true and earnest, one's whole mind must be fixed on Buddha-recitation and seeking rebirth; only then can they be called true and earnest. If one recites the Buddha's name on the one hand and on the other gives rise to thoughts of dust and turbidity, then one's vows and practice are not true and earnest. Therefore, for the one who recites the Buddha's name, even if the cutting off of thoughts is not easy to accomplish, the two lines ‘they should not give rise to a mind dwelling in form, nor give rise to a mind dwelling in sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas’ must by all means be carried out. Otherwise, one's vows are not earnest and one's practice is not true—how could one be received and guided by the Buddha? Why? Because the breath of dust and turbidity is heavy and accords all too little with the word ‘purity,’ and then even the Buddha can do nothing for one!”

[Reciting without reciting] To recite the Buddha's name by way of no-thought (not a single thought arising)—this is reciting the Buddha of true character, the recitation of the dharma-body Buddha. (For details see the article
“Reciting Without Reciting”

They should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere”: to know that all dharmas are illusion, and to be neither dragged, nor bound, nor turned by them—this is what the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch means when it says:
“Cause the six consciousnesses to go out through the six gates, and amid the six dusts be neither defiled nor mixed; coming and going freely, in general use without obstruction.”
The Record of the Mirror of the Source says:

“Chan Master Anguo said: The sutra says, ‘They should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere.’ Dwelling nowhere means: not dwelling in form, not dwelling in sound, not dwelling in delusion, not dwelling in awakening, not dwelling in essence, not dwelling in function. And ‘giving rise to the mind’ means: in all places, revealing the one mind. If one dwells in good and gives rise to mind, good appears; if one dwells in evil and gives rise to mind, evil appears; and the original mind is then hidden and lost. If one dwells nowhere, the worlds of the ten directions are only the one mind. Believe and know that ‘it was not the wind or the banner that moved; it was the mind that moved.’”
The Great Compendium of a Hundred Commentaries on the Diamond Sutra says:

“The mind of beings originally dwells nowhere; because conditions come and touch it, the mind is then produced. Not knowing that the conditions touched are empty, one takes the world's dharmas to be real, and so dwells the mind upon conditions. This is just like a monkey grasping at the moon
(the moon in the water)
, or a diseased eye seeing flowers
(flowers in the sky)

: all the ten thousand dharmas are born from the mind. If one awakens to the true nature, one dwells nowhere. The mind that dwells nowhere is wisdom, free of all affliction, like great space, without any obstruction. The mind that dwells on something is deluded thought; the six dusts contend and arise, like floating clouds coming and going without fixedness.”
Question: If one does not give rise to mind, how can one live and work?

Answer: Not giving rise to mind means not giving rise to mind by clinging to marks; that is, giving rise to mind without clinging to marks (not taking conditions and objects as real). When affairs come, attend to them; when affairs go, be still. In doing things, do not cling to marks (do not take conditions and objects as real; within the dream, know it is a dream), act according to principle, with single-minded devotion, without giving rise to deluded thoughts.

Subhuti! Suppose there were a person whose body were like the king of Mount Sumeru: what do you think, is that body great? Subhuti said: Very great, World-Honored One! Why? The Buddha says it is no body; therefore it is called a great body.

The Buddha asked: Subhuti! Suppose there were a person whose body were like the king of Mount Sumeru: what do you think, is this body great? Subhuti answered: Exceedingly great, World-Honored One! Why is this body said to be exceedingly great? Because this body is illusion (the Buddha says it is no body), and so greatness and smallness can be spoken of (greatness and smallness are concepts within the dream of ignorance).

[King of Mount Sumeru] That is, Mount Sumeru. Because it is the highest and greatest, and is made of the four treasures gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal, and no other mountain can compare with it, it is the king of mountains and is therefore called the king of Mount Sumeru. “Mount Sumeru” is rendered in Chinese as Wondrous High Mountain, and is the center of a small world. [A body like the king of Mount Sumeru] A body as tall, great, wondrous, and fair as Mount Sumeru. The “body” here is the supreme wondrous reward-body, the body of boundless excellent marks that a bodhisattva can realize only after diligently cultivating the six perfections and ten thousand practices through many kalpas, with merit and wisdom complete. This body is subtle: though it has form and marks, none but a bodhisattva on the grounds can see it. (From the first-abiding bodhisattva up to the Buddha, all have three bodies: the dharma-body, the reward-body, and the response-body.)

The World-Honored One has just taught the rule of the pure mind (“they should not give rise to a mind dwelling in form, nor give rise to a mind dwelling in sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas; they should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere”), and now he tosses out this topic of the supreme wondrous reward-body, of such interest to cultivators, to see how well Subhuti has grasped and mastered this rule of the pure mind. Subhuti's first sentence, “Exceedingly great,” is like a mirror reflecting an object—this is right. In the second sentence he says at once that this body is illusion, closely guarding the original mind and not dragged by conditions. This shows that the Elder Subhuti has not only understood the rule of the pure mind but applies it well, setting us an example: thought after thought, abiding in the Way.

The Blue Cliff Record relates: Mazu and his disciple Baizhang were walking together when they saw a wild duck fly past. The Patriarch said: What is that? Baizhang said: A wild duck. The Patriarch said: Where has it gone (testing whether Baizhang had given rise to a mind dwelling in form)? Baizhang said: It has flown away. The Patriarch then twisted Baizhang's nose, and Baizhang cried out in pain. The Patriarch said: When did it ever fly away! At these words Baizhang had an awakening.

Baizhang's first reply, “a wild duck,” was like a mirror reflecting an object—this was right. But the second sentence, “it has flown away,” was giving rise to a mind dwelling in form, following conditions and chasing objects, failing to guard the original mind (losing right mindfulness). So Mazu twisted his nose, wanting him to turn back and guard the original mind. In the midst of the pain Baizhang heard his master say: When did it ever fly away? (The wild duck is illusion—where is there any coming or going?) And he suddenly awakened: “One should thus give rise to the pure mind.” (Mazu twisted Baizhang's nose precisely to make him never forget to guard the original mind and never follow conditions and chase objects.)
[When did it ever fly away] Gathering marks back into the nature, and taking them as empty.
All marks whatsoever are false and vain.”

If one is not detached from marks, it is difficult to awaken to the Way; hence Mazu used the thunderbolt method, swift as lightning that leaves no time to stop the ears, to flash-strike Baizhang's unawakened mind. The Vajra Samādhi Sūtra says:
“‘If one loses the original mind, one should at once repent’—this dharma is coolness and refreshment.”
From this one may glimpse the conduct of a strict master and a lofty disciple, and feel intimately that “the fragrance of plum blossoms comes from bitter cold.”

blocks.text: Chapter Eleven: The Merit of the Unconditioned Is Supreme

inline.s: Above, the unconditioned dharma was taught (they should not give rise to a mind dwelling in form, nor give rise to a mind dwelling in sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas; they should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere). This section says that receiving and upholding this sutra and practicing while detached from marks—the unconditioned dharma—brings merit that is utterly supreme.

Subhuti! Suppose all the grains of sand in the Ganges River, and as many Ganges Rivers as those grains of sand: what do you think, are the grains of sand in all those Ganges Rivers not many? Subhuti said: Very many, World-Honored One! Even the Ganges Rivers alone are countless in number, how much more their grains of sand.

The World-Honored One asked: Subhuti! Take all the sand in the Ganges River, and let each grain of sand be one Ganges River: what do you think, are the grains of sand in all those Ganges Rivers not many? (Mathematically speaking, suppose the number of grains of sand in one Ganges River is
N
, then the number of “the grains of sand in all those Ganges Rivers” is:
N
times
N
.) Subhuti answered: Very many indeed; the Ganges Rivers alone (
N
) are already countless in number, how much more the grains of sand in those Ganges Rivers (
N
times
N
Master Kumarajiva's translation is superb! Not only is the language concise and apt, but it rises and falls with cadence and reads aloud beautifully.

Subhuti! I now tell you in truth. If there were good men and good women who filled with the seven treasures as many three-thousand-great-thousand worlds as there are grains of sand in all those Ganges Rivers, and gave them away, would the merit they obtain be great? Subhuti said: Very great, World-Honored One!

Subhuti! I now tell you in truth. If there were good men and good women who gave in charity the seven treasures of as many three-thousand-great-thousand worlds as could be filled with all the grains of sand in those Ganges Rivers of yours (
N
times
N
)—would the merit obtained be great? Subhuti answered: Very great, World-Honored One.

[I now tell you in truth] In “I now tell you in truth,” what follows “you” should be a period, and the meaning runs right through to the end of this section: “and this merit surpasses the former merit.”
The Buddha told Subhuti: If good men and good women, within this sutra, receive and uphold even a four-line verse and expound it for others, this merit surpasses the former merit.
The Buddha told Subhuti: If there are good men and good women who, within this sutra, receive and uphold even a four-line verse and expound it for others, this merit surpasses the former merit.

This says that however many the seven treasures may be, it is still giving with marks; whereas receiving and upholding this sutra and expounding it for others is giving without marks, and so the merit is all the greater.

blocks.text: Chapter Twelve: Honoring the Right Teaching

inline.s: The World-Honored One further teaches the supreme excellence of this sutra. “The right teaching” means the Buddha's teaching in this sutra.

Furthermore, Subhuti! Wherever this sutra is expounded, even a four-line verse or so, you should know that place: all the heavenly beings, humans, and asuras of every world should make offerings there, as to a Buddha's stupa or temple. How much more so if someone can receive, uphold, read, and recite the whole of it.

Not only that (continuing from the passage above), Subhuti! Whenever and wherever and for whatever reason this Diamond Sutra is expounded, whether in whole or in part, even as few as four lines, you should know that the place where it is expounded is most honored and rare, and that all the heavenly beings, humans, and asuras of every world (the three good paths) should come there to protect the Dharma and make offerings, as to a Buddha's stupa or temple. If merely expounding four lines brings merit such as this, how much more so if someone can receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra in its entirety.

[Wherever it is expounded] Whenever, wherever, and for whatever reason it is expounded. [Heavenly beings, humans, and asuras] Heavenly beings, humans, and asuras—these are the three good paths of the world. [Asura] One of the six paths, rendered in Chinese as “non-heaven,” because such beings have the blessings of heaven but not the virtues of heaven: they are like heavenly beings yet are not heavenly beings.
Subhuti! You should know that such a person accomplishes the most supreme, foremost, and rarest dharma. Wherever this sutra is, there is the Buddha, and there is a reverent disciple.

Subhuti! You should know that such a person will accomplish the most supreme, foremost, and rarest anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi dharma. Wherever this Diamond Sutra is, it is as if the Buddha were here, and one should honor it as disciples honor the Buddha.
[And there is a reverent disciple] “A reverent disciple” means honoring as disciples honor the Buddha. The Northern Wei

translation by Bodhiruci reads: “Subhuti! You should know that such a person accomplishes the most supreme, foremost, and rarest dharma. Wherever this sutra is, there is the Buddha, and there is one who honors him as the Buddha.”

The above shows that receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting the Diamond Sutra, expounding the Diamond Sutra, and the place where the Diamond Sutra is—all are supremely honored and rare beyond compare, making one understand the surpassing excellence of this dharma-gate of becoming a Buddha by detachment from illusion.

blocks.text: Chapter Thirteen: Receiving and Upholding in Accord with the Dharma

inline.s: Receiving and upholding in accord with the Dharma”—the “in accord with the Dharma” is: “All marks whatsoever are false and vain. If one sees all marks as no marks, one sees the Tathāgata.”

Then Subhuti said to the Buddha: World-Honored One! What should this sutra be named? How should we receive and uphold it? The Buddha told Subhuti: This sutra is named the Diamond Prajñā-Pāramitā. By this name you should receive and uphold it.

At that time Subhuti asked the Buddha: World-Honored One! What should this sutra be named? How should we receive and uphold it? The Buddha told Subhuti: This sutra is named the Diamond Prajñā-Pāramitā. You should receive and uphold it according to this sutra's name—the Diamond Prajñā-Pāramitā (reaching the other shore of nirvāṇa by the diamond-like wondrous wisdom). For this is the mind-dharma that enables you to become a Buddha by detachment from illusion through diamond-like wondrous wisdom.

The core of practice is detachment from illusion, and so below the World-Honored One lists in turn that prajñā-pāramitā is illusion, that the Tathāgata's teaching of Dharma is illusion, that minute dust is illusion, that the world is illusion, and that the thirty-two marks are also illusion. At the end, this section closes with the immeasurable merit of receiving and upholding this sutra, showing that illusion is not wholly nothing: it has no substance but has marks, lest those who misunderstand fall into the abyss of annihilationism.

In this sutra the World-Honored One teaches again and again that all is illusion, wanting us neither to cling to existence (clinging to marks) nor to cling to nothingness (annihilating marks), but to borrow the false to cultivate the true, and to use illusion to transcend illusion. Yet beings, since the beginningless kalpa, life after life, either cling to existence or cling to nothingness, so heavy is the habitual taint that, though they now understand in principle, the moment a condition appears they are deluded again. Therefore the World-Honored One wants us to use diamond-like wisdom to contemplate and examine ourselves, to contemplate and examine amid conditions and objects, closely and without interruption, turning delusion into awakening, reaching the other shore of nirvāṇa, and waking from the dream of ignorance. The Sixth Patriarch said: “In the dark house of affliction, one must always give rise to the sun of wisdom.” This sun of wisdom is the diamond prajñā.
Why is this? Subhuti! What the Buddha speaks of as prajñā-pāramitā is not prajñā-pāramitā; therefore it is called prajñā-pāramitā.

The World-Honored One continued: What is the reason for this? Because “all marks whatsoever are false and vain,” even prajñā-pāramitā itself is illusion (breaking the mark of dharmas). In this dream of ignorance, there is not one thing that is not illusion, and so one must quickly escape by the diamond prajñā-pāramitā.

Lest beings fail to understand and again take prajñā-pāramitā as real, cultivating while clinging to marks and thinking there is a prajñā-pāramitā to cultivate and a nirvāṇa to obtain, the World-Honored One repeated with care: Subhuti! The prajñā-pāramitā spoken of by the Buddha is likewise illusion. The Complete Enlightenment Sutra says: “All bodhisattvas and the beings of the last age should keep far from all illusory and false realms. Because they firmly hold to the mind of detachment, the mind, being like an illusion, is also to be detached from; the detachment itself being illusion, it too is to be detached from; the detachment from that detachment being illusion, it too is to be detached from; when one reaches having nothing more to detach from, all illusions are removed.” This says: toward all illusory and false realms one should firmly hold to the mind of detachment; but the mind is illusion, so the mind of detachment must also be detached from; the detachment of the “mind of detachment” is also illusion, so this detachment must also be detached from; and this detachment is also illusion, so it too must be detached from; until one reaches having nothing more to detach from, and all illusions are removed. Therefore detachment from illusion must be carried out layer by layer, until one reaches having nothing more to detach from; only then can all illusions be extinguished. Hence the ancients said: “Set up and break down as you go; fall into neither of the two extremes.”

The prajñā-pāramitā spoken of by the Buddha is to reach nirvāṇa and accomplish the Buddha-way by prajñā wisdom detached from marks. But if one again takes prajñā-pāramitā as real and cultivates while clinging to marks (a conditioned dharma), then one can never reach the other shore of nirvāṇa. The principle that the earlier scripture sets forth again and again goes one layer deeper here. This is what is meant by “Only exhaust (do away with) ordinary sentiment; there is no other sage understanding.” From this too one can sense the Buddha's compassion and painstaking care for beings. Therefore the Elder Subhuti praised him, saying: “The Tathāgata well guards and keeps in mind all bodhisattvas, well entrusts all bodhisattvas.”
The Great Prajñā-Pāramitā Sūtra

Volume Five Hundred Forty-eight says: “The Heaven King should know that the dharma I have realized is prajñā-pāramitā. This dharma is most profound: there is no realizer and nothing realized, no place of realization and no time of realization.” The Great Prajñā-Pāramitā Sūtra

Volume Four Hundred Sixteen says: “How should a bodhisattva and great bodhisattva keep far from all clinging to dharmas? Good Manifestation (that is, Subhuti), if a bodhisattva and great bodhisattva contemplates the natures of all dharmas as all like empty space and unattainable, this is how a bodhisattva and great bodhisattva should keep far from all clinging to dharmas.” The Great Prajñā-Pāramitā Sūtra
Volume One

Chapter on Learning and Contemplation says: “All bodhisattvas and great bodhisattvas should, with non-attachment as the skillful means, perfect prajñā-pāramitā, because the natures and marks of all dharmas are unattainable.”
Subhuti! What do you think? Has the Tathāgata said any dharma? Subhuti said to the Buddha: World-Honored One! The Tathāgata has said nothing.
The World-Honored One asked: Subhuti! What do you think, has the Tathāgata taught any dharma? Subhuti answered: World-Honored One! The Tathāgata has not said any dharma.

The Buddha taught and expounded the Dharma for forty-nine years, yet he says he has not said any dharma. This has several deep meanings. First, the Tathāgata's teaching of Dharma is an affair within the dream of ignorance and is not truly existent. Second, the Tathāgata's teaching of Dharma points at the moon with a finger and is not the dharma itself; one must not stick to the words but should take up the meaning beyond the words. Third, all Buddhas of the ten directions and three times teach in just this way; Buddhas are one in the Way and dharmas are all like this—it is not the World-Honored One's own invention. Fourth, the World-Honored One has no intention to fabricate: he speaks without speaking.

Even so, the Tathāgata's teaching of Dharma can lead beings out of illusion: “Therefore, one should not grasp at dharmas, nor grasp at non-dharmas.” The World-Honored One's teaching is a road; the cultivator must walk along the road to have real benefit.

Prajñā-pāramitā is illusion, and the Tathāgata's teaching of Dharma is also illusion. Though both are illusion, we must use them to transcend illusion, using them without clinging. Here the World-Honored One again clarifies transcending illusion by illusion.

Subhuti! What do you think? Are all the minute dust-motes of a three-thousand-great-thousand world many? Subhuti said: Very many, World-Honored One! Subhuti! The Tathāgata says all minute dust-motes are not minute dust-motes; therefore they are called minute dust-motes. The Tathāgata says the world is not the world; therefore it is called the world.

The Buddha asked: Subhuti! What do you think, are all the minute dust-motes of a three-thousand-great-thousand world many? Subhuti answered: Very many, World-Honored One! The Buddha said: Subhuti! All minute dust-motes (having marks), the Tathāgata says are not minute dust-motes (no substance); therefore they are called minute dust-motes (are illusion). The Tathāgata says the world (having marks) is not the world (no substance); therefore it is called the world (is illusion).
This says that minute dust-motes (the small) are illusion, and the world (the great) is also illusion.

Subhuti! What do you think? Can one see the Tathāgata by the thirty-two marks? No, World-Honored One! One cannot see the Tathāgata by the thirty-two marks. Why? What the Tathāgata says are the thirty-two marks are not marks; therefore they are called the thirty-two marks.

The Buddha asked: Subhuti! What do you think, can one see the Tathāgata by the thirty-two marks? Subhuti answered: One cannot, World-Honored One! One cannot see the Tathāgata by the thirty-two marks. Why? What the Tathāgata says are the thirty-two marks (having marks) are not the thirty-two marks (no substance); therefore they are called the thirty-two marks (are illusion).
This says that although the thirty-two marks are the most supreme and wondrous bodily marks, they are also illusion. In the Great Prajñā-Pāramitā Sūtra

Volume Twenty-five, the Buddha says: “When a bodhisattva and great bodhisattva is mindful of the Buddha, he is not mindful by the thirty-two marks, nor does he contemplate the golden body, nor the fathom of light, nor the eighty secondary marks. Why? Because the Buddha-body is without self-nature.”

[The thirty-two marks] Also called the thirty-two marks of a great being. When the inner virtue of a Buddha or a wheel-turning sage king is manifested in bodily marks, there are thirty-two of them, from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head, not one of which is other than supreme and wondrous.

Subhuti! If good men and good women give in charity their bodies and lives as many times as the sands of the Ganges; and if again someone, within this sutra, receives and upholds even a four-line verse and expounds it for others, the latter's merit is far greater.

The Buddha said: Subhuti! If good men and good women give in charity their bodies and lives as many times as the grains of sand of the Ganges, the merit they obtain is far less than that of one who, within this sutra, receives and upholds even a single verse (four lines) and expounds it for others.
[Give in charity bodies and lives as many times as the sands of the Ganges] Giving one's life as many times as the grains of sand of the Ganges (in one lifetime there is only one life).

Within the dream of ignorance, all dharmas are illusion. Prajñā-pāramitā is illusion, the dharma the Tathāgata teaches is illusion, and even minute dust-motes, the world, and the Buddha's thirty-two marks are all illusion; therefore receiving and upholding this sutra and understanding the unconditioned dharma, detached from marks and dwelling nowhere, brings immeasurable merit.

blocks.text: Chapter Fourteen: Detached from Marks, Still and Extinct

inline.s: Without affliction is called “still”; without birth and death is called “extinct.” The state without affliction and without birth and death is nirvāṇa. “Detached from marks, still and extinct” is what the scripture below says: “Detached from all marks, one is named a Buddha.”

Then, when Subhuti had heard this sutra expounded, he understood its meaning and purport deeply, and with tears of grief and joy he said to the Buddha: Rare indeed, World-Honored One! The Buddha has expounded a sutra so profoundly deep. From of old, though I have obtained the wisdom-eye, I had never heard such a sutra.

At that time Subhuti, having heard the wondrous principle taught by the World-Honored One, deeply understood the meaning and purport of this sutra, and with grief and joy mingled and tears of gratitude, praised the Buddha: ‘Incomparably supreme, World-Honored One! You have expounded a sutra so profound, subtle, and penetrating. From of old, though I have realized the wisdom-eye, I had never heard such a sutra!’

[A profoundly deep sutra] This says that the theory, method, and realm of this sutra are utterly profound, subtle, and penetrating. [Wisdom-eye] The eye of wisdom, realized by the two vehicles, the wisdom that knows the equal nature and emptiness of all dharmas. [Nature is empty] All things and dharmas are by nature originally empty, with no substantial reality to be obtained.

What was it that made Subhuti so filled with mingled grief and joy and tears of gratitude? His joy was that today he had heard the most perfect, sudden, and true dharma of becoming a Buddha, and so the Elder says below, in deep understanding of its meaning and purport: “Detached from all marks, one is named a Buddha.” His grief was that since the beginningless kalpa he had had no way to hear the great dharma, and so had sunk down until today. The Elder could not stop rejoicing!
Chen

Paramārtha's translation reads: “At that time the pure-lived Subhuti, because the benefit of the dharma was swift, at once wept aloud.” The Diamond Sutra is a swift dharma; this is the practice of the One Buddha Vehicle: seeing the nature (“if one sees all marks as no marks, one sees the Tathāgata”) and eliminating habit (“they should not give rise to a mind dwelling in form, nor give rise to a mind dwelling in sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas; they should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere”), detached from all marks, directly realizing Buddhahood (“detached from all marks, one is named a Buddha”).
[A swift dharma] A rapid and sudden dharma.

The theory, realm, and method taught in this sutra are suited not only to beginners (“after the Tathāgata's extinction, in the last five hundred years, there will be those who keep the precepts and cultivate merit,” who can believe, accept, and practice it), but run straight through to the Buddha-fruit: awakening to the unconditioned dharma, without passing through the various stages (without passing through the fifty-two stages), directly realizing Buddhahood. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch records: “The Master (the Fifth Patriarch Hongren) constantly urged monks and laypeople alike simply to uphold the Diamond Sutra, and then they would see their own nature and directly realize Buddhahood.” Truly:
The unsurpassed, profound, and wondrous Dharma, in hundreds of thousands of kalpas hard to encounter,

World-Honored One! If again there are people who hear this sutra with pure faith, then the true character is born in them. You should know that such a person accomplishes the foremost and rarest merit. World-Honored One! This true character is no character; therefore the Tathāgata names it the true character.

World-Honored One! If again there are people who hear this sutra with pure faith, then the true character is born in them. You should know that such a person accomplishes the foremost and rarest merit.”

—Subhuti continued: World-Honored One! If there are still other people who hear this sutra with pure faith, they at once realize the true character (the actual state of affairs in which all things in the universe are illusion). You should know that such a person accomplishes the most supreme merit.

[If again there are people] If there are still other people. This closely follows the passage above: I, Subhuti, have heard this sutra expounded, deeply understood its meaning and purport, and benefited beyond compare; if there are still other people who hear this sutra, . . . [Faith] The mind that gives rise to belief in the dharma heard, deeply believing without doubt. [Pure faith] Hearing this sutra and deeply believing without doubt, one thereupon sees illusion and at once detaches from it, and amid conditions and objects closely examines (not giving rise to a mind dwelling in form, not giving rise to a mind dwelling in sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas, giving rise to a mind that dwells nowhere); the clouds of delusion scatter, the light of the nature shows, and the mind attains purity. [True character] The true character is the actual state of affairs in which “all dharmas are ultimately empty, nothing whatsoever.” In the Buddha Treasury Sutra

Chapter Two, on Buddha-Recitation, the Buddha says: “What is named the true character of all dharmas? All dharmas are ultimately empty, nothing whatsoever.” [Then the true character is born] That is, one realizes in person the actual state of affairs in which all things in the universe are illusion. The Complete Enlightenment Sutra says: “Within the true character, there truly are no bodhisattvas and no beings. Why? Bodhisattvas and beings are all illusory transformations.” In the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra
Volume Forty

Chapter on Kaundinya, the Buddha says: “All dharmas are false; wherever they cease, that is named the real, is named the true character, is named the dharma-realm, is named ultimate wisdom, is named the truth of the supreme meaning, is named the emptiness of the supreme meaning.” [Foremost and rarest] Most supreme; here “rare” means supreme.

The work of the Buddhadharma lies entirely in awakening—in the birth of the true character. In the Buddha Treasury Sutra the Buddha says: “The true character of all dharmas, ultimately empty and still—this is the Buddha-way.” The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says: “The thought before is deluded: one is an ordinary being; the thought after is awakened: one is a Buddha. The thought before clings to conditions: that is affliction; the thought after is detached from conditions: that is bodhi.” This sutra says: “All marks whatsoever are false and vain. If one sees all marks as no marks, one sees the Tathāgata.”
World-Honored One! This true character is no character; therefore the Tathāgata names it the true character.”
—Next, Subhuti says: World-Honored One! This true character is without marks (the true character is without marks); therefore the Tathāgata says it is the true character.
This is the emptiness of the supreme meaning—the emptiness of the middle-way true character that is neither empty nor existent, where even the true character is not clung to.
In the Buddha Treasury Sutra

Chapter One, on the True Character of All Dharmas, the Buddha says: “All dharmas are neither born nor ceasing, without marks and without doing.” This looks at all dharmas from the standpoint of substance. To one within the dream of ignorance, all dharmas have marks; but to one whose eyes are open, there is nothing at all. The Direct Explanation of the True Mind says: “It is like a person with diseased eyes who sees flowers in the sky. Or a person without disease says: There are no sky-flowers. The sick person does not believe it. When the eye-disease is gone, the sky-flowers vanish of themselves, and only then does he believe the flowers were not there.” Beings, within the utterly still non-arising, see only arising and ceasing (marks); the Buddhas, within the manifest arising and ceasing, see only the non-arising (no marks).
[The true character is without marks] The Great Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom

Volume Fourteen says: “If one leaves home and keeps the precepts, does not manage worldly affairs, and constantly contemplates the true character of all dharmas as without marks, then though at first one's faculties are dull, they gradually become sharp. Through various such causes and conditions, this is named the keeping of precepts giving rise to prajñā-pāramitā. Through such things, this is named the perfection of morality giving rise to the six perfections.”
[The perfection of morality] The perfection of keeping the precepts.

World-Honored One! I now hear such a sutra, and to believe, understand, receive, and uphold it is not difficult. But in a future age, in the last five hundred years, if there are beings who hear this sutra and believe, understand, receive, and uphold it, such a person is foremost and rarest.

Subhuti continued: World-Honored One! I now hear such a profoundly deep sutra, and to believe, understand, receive, and uphold it is not difficult. But if in the fifth five hundred years after the Tathāgata's extinction and thereafter, there are beings who hear this sutra and believe, understand, receive, and uphold it, such a person is foremost and supreme.

[In a future age, in the last five hundred years] This means the same as “after the Tathāgata's extinction, in the last five hundred years” in the sixth section: the fifth five hundred years after the Tathāgata's extinction and thereafter. [If there are beings] If there are beings. “If” is a conjunction, equivalent to “in case” or “supposing.”

Why? Such a person has no mark of a self, no mark of a human, no mark of a being, no mark of a life. Why is this? The mark of a self is no mark; the mark of a human, the mark of a being, and the mark of a life are no marks. Why? Detached from all marks, one is named a Buddha.
This passage of scripture clarifies why “such a person is foremost and rarest.”

Why? Such a person has no mark of a self, no mark of a human, no mark of a being, no mark of a life. Why is this? The mark of a self is no mark; the mark of a human, the mark of a being, and the mark of a life are no marks.”

—Why is such a person foremost and supreme? Because he no longer has the mark of a self, the mark of a human, the mark of a being, or the mark of a life. Why has he no mark of a self, mark of a human, mark of a being, or mark of a life? Because the mark of a self (having marks) is no mark of a self (no substance), and the mark of a self is illusion; the mark of a human, the mark of a being, and the mark of a life (having marks) are no mark of a human, no mark of a being, no mark of a life (no substance), and the mark of a human, the mark of a being, and the mark of a life are illusion.

This says: because such a person believes, understands, receives, and upholds this sutra, and has put “all marks whatsoever are false and vain” into practice in his own thought, speech, and action, these illusory four marks should no longer be present.
Why? Detached from all marks, one is named a Buddha.”
—Why is such a person said to be foremost and supreme? Because, detached from all marks,
one is named a Buddha.
[One is named a Buddha] That is, one is named a Buddha. Here “a” functions like “of,” as in: “Can you serve him?”
